papers.title_in_file: Time, Cost, Efficiency: ResNet50 Quantum TL, TL Models, 2 Datasets
papers.what_it_is: A four-page vendor slide report (ChemicalQDevice, 13 August 2023) comparing runtime, cost and efficiency of ResNet50 transfer learning and a 4- or 17-qubit quantum transfer learning model on CPU, TPU, V100 and A100 Colab runtimes.

assertions.value: The authors state that all runs used 10 epochs and High RAM, and list Colab credits per hour as 0.19 for CPU, 2.05 for TPU, 5.64 for V100 and 13.08 for A100.
quotes: All Runs: 10 Epochs, High RAM. Colab Credits/Hr: CPU = 0.19, TPU = 2.05, V1004 = 5.64, A1005 = 13.08.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own run setup in the Table 1 footer.

assertions.value: The authors state a Colab rate of $0.100 per credit and that the quantum transfer learning model uses the Default.qubit quantum simulator, so the quantum part was simulated and not run on quantum hardware.
quotes: Colab Rate = $0.100/Credit.6 QTL Model Utilizes Default.qubit Quantum Simulator.7
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own setup in the Table 1 footer.
assertions.reader_inference: A simulator on classical CPU, TPU or GPU runtimes was used; no result concerns quantum hardware.

assertions.value: The authors list hourly rates of $0.019 for CPU, $0.205 for TPU, $0.564 for V100 and $1.308 for A100.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the rates it used for cost in the Table 1 headers.

assertions.value: The authors define cost as runtime times rate, and efficiency as 1 divided by the product of runtime and cost.
quotes: CPU Cost (Runtime *Rate)
CPU Efficiency 1/(Runtime
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the cost and efficiency metrics in the Table 1 headers.
assertions.reader_inference: Efficiency scales with the inverse of runtime squared times rate, so it favours fast runtimes strongly.

assertions.value: The authors state the goal as comparing runtimes, costs and efficiencies of two transfer learning methods across two datasets on four computing methods, and state that runtimes and costs were based on model type, number of classes, number of images, batch size and whether a quantum algorithm was used.
quotes: Compare runtimes, costs, and efficiencies of two transfer learning methods across two datasets utilizing four different computing methods
run times and costs to evaluate efficiencies were primarily based on model type, number of classes, number of images, batch size, and whether a quantum algorithm was used.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own goal and measurement scope on p.3.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper reports one run per cell and no repeats or variance.

assertions.value: The authors report that for 10 epochs the CPU method was the most cost effective across all model combinations, with costs from $0.003 to $0.044, and the most efficient for the quantum transfer learning model.
assertions.anchor: Cost and Benefits, p.3; Table 1, p.1
quotes: For 10 epochs, the CPU processing method was the most cost effective method across all model combinations ranging from $0.003-$0.044
was the most efficient method for the quantum transfer learning model.
assertions.certainty_reason: A single-run empirical result from one vendor report.
assertions.reader_inference: On a CPU the simulated quantum model costs little because the rate is low, so cost favours the simulator on the slowest hardware.

assertions.value: The authors predict that greater optimization of hybrid computing by industry experts will likely decrease both time and costs for greater efficiency in quantum models, and that better fine tuning of CPU, GPU and multi-GPU quantum simulators in cloud platforms will likely increase adoption and decrease costs.

improved fine tuning of CPU/GPU/Multi-GPU quantum simulators in cloud based compute platforms will also likely increase adoption rates and decrease costs.

assertions.value: The authors claim that quantum machine learning will likely offer fields such as medical informatics new utilities and higher accuracies due to processing datasets with qubits or qudits, and that emerging quantum computers with less noise may offer speed ups in the future.
